question: records
reviewed_by: Claude (claude-opus-5-5), 2026-10-10; every quote checked against open-us-law v2026.09.1

reader_notes.Scope: only § 149.43 is modelled: Scope: only § 149.43 is used. Most of its text is the division (A) definitions and exemption list, which are not shown one by one. The court of claims procedure (§ 2743.75) is not printed.
reader_notes.No fixed response deadline: records must: No fixed response deadline: records must be 'promptly prepared' for inspection and copies made 'within a reasonable period of time' (B)(1), and mailed copies sent 'within a reasonable period of time after receiving the request' (B)(7)(a). The act has no deemed-denial rule. A public records policy 'may not establish a fixed period of time before it will respond' unless it is less than eight hours (E)(2). A failure to respond promptly or within a reasonable time lets the requester serve a (C)(1) complaint, and supports attorney's fees under (C)(4)(b)(i).
reader_notes.Ambiguous or overly broad requests (B)(2: Ambiguous or overly broad requests (B)(2): the office may deny but must explain how its records are kept and accessed so the requester can revise; the requester may instead serve a (C)(1) complaint. The statute does not say whether this first denial also needs a (B)(3) explanation, which applies to a request 'ultimately denied'.
reader_notes.Denials and redactions:: Denials and redactions: any denial, in part or in whole, needs an explanation with legal authority, in writing if the request was written, and the office may later rely on additional reasons in court (B)(3). A redaction is a denial of the redacted information unless federal or state law authorizes or requires it (B)(1); an authorized redaction is not a denial. The statute does not order the explanation and the release, and it does not say whether a redaction of information exempt under (A)(1) is itself 'authorized' by state law.
reader_notes.Costs: inspection carries no general fee: Costs: inspection carries no general fee, except that law enforcement agencies and prosecutors may charge the actual cost of preparing video records for inspection or copying, up to $75 per hour of video and $750 total, and victims who give the affidavit are exempt (B)(1), (B)(11). Copies are 'at cost' (B)(1), on paper, the medium the office keeps the record on, or another medium it can reasonably use, at the requester's choice (B)(6). The office may require advance payment of copy costs, postage, delivery and supplies (B)(6), (B)(7)(a). A policy may limit mailed or digital deliveries to ten per month unless the requester certifies a non-commercial purpose (B)(7)(c); 'commercial' is narrowly construed. For video records an estimate is due within five business days, and if the office's policy requires prepayment, the duty to produce begins only on payment in full. lexflow treats a missed five-business-day estimate as a division (B) failure that opens the complaint route; the statute states no other consequence. The statute does not say whether the estimate comes before the response.
reader_notes.Requesters with special rules: Requesters with special rules: incarcerated persons have no right to criminal investigation or prosecution records unless the sentencing judge finds the information necessary to support a justiciable claim (B)(8). Journalists may obtain certain information about designated public service workers by a signed written request stating the public interest (B)(9). Victims may obtain depictions of themselves (B)(10). The auditor of state may redirect requests for audit records to the original office (B)(1).
reader_notes.Pre-suit complaint (C)(1): Pre-suit complaint (C)(1): the aggrieved person must serve a complaint on the court of claims form under Civ. R. 4. The office then has three business days to cure, and the requester 'shall not file' within that period; (C)(2) adds that the complaint must have been transmitted 'at least three business days before the filing of the suit'. The office may 'cure or otherwise address the failure'; addressing it without satisfying the requester does not shorten that wait. The end of the three days ends only the pre-suit window, not the office's chance to cure later.
reader_notes.One remedy, not both (C)(1): One remedy, not both (C)(1): the requester may file either a complaint with the clerk of the court of claims or common pleas under § 2743.75, or a mandamus action in common pleas, the court of appeals, or the supreme court. Each must be filed with a written affirmation that the complaint was served, the failure is unresolved, and at least three business days passed (C)(2); without it the suit 'shall be dismissed'.
reader_notes.Mandamus remedies (C)(3)-(6): Mandamus remedies (C)(3)-(6) are shown as tables of their own, outside the office's steps, because the court acts outside the office's process: statutory damages; court costs (mandatory to the relator on a compliance order or a (C)(4)(b)(iii) bad-faith finding, and the office may recover costs and expenses if a denied writ was frivolous, (C)(4)(a), (C)(6)); and attorney's fees (discretionary on a compliance order or a (C)(4)(b)(i)-(iii) ground, barred when both (C)(4)(c) well-informed-office conditions hold, and the office's fees if frivolous). The (C)(5) limits on fees (only fees incurred before release plus fees litigating the fees, reducible where an alternative means should have been pursued) are summarised, not set out in the tables.

gaps: Scope: only § 149.43 is modelled, but it alone is about 10,600 words, far above the benchmark budget; it cannot be shortened because the request duties (B), the remedies (C) and the policy rules (E) are all in this one section. Most of the text is the division (A) definitions and exemption list, which feed the all_exempt and some_exempt inputs but are not modelled rule by rule. The court of claims procedure (§ 2743.75) is not printed; the model ends at claims_complaint.

No fixed response deadline: records must be 'promptly prepared' for inspection and copies made 'within a reasonable period of time' (B)(1), and mailed copies sent 'within a reasonable period of time after receiving the request' (B)(7)(a). The act has no deemed-denial rule, so respond carries no timer. A public records policy 'may not establish a fixed period of time before it will respond' unless it is less than eight hours (E)(2). A failure to respond promptly or within a reasonable time is modelled as the 'aggrieved' branch straight from submit_request to serve_complaint (C)(1); it is a condition, not a timer, because the statute sets no period. The same failure supports attorney's fees under (C)(4)(b)(i).

Who may request and how: any person may ask, orally or in writing. The office may ask for a written request, the requester's identity or the intended use only after saying that none is mandatory and how it would help (B)(5). Requiring identity or intended use, unless law requires or authorizes it, 'constitutes a denial of the request' (B)(4); this is the first response_type rule.

Ambiguous or overly broad requests (B)(2): the office may deny but must explain how its records are kept and accessed so the requester can revise. A revised request goes back to respond (exclusive merge, join 'any'); the requester may instead serve a (C)(1) complaint, or the request ends at ambiguous_request_denied. The statute does not say whether this first denial also needs a (B)(3) explanation, which applies to a request 'ultimately denied'.

Denials and redactions: any denial, in part or in whole, needs an explanation with legal authority, in writing if the request was written, and the office may later rely on additional reasons in court (B)(3). A redaction is a denial of the redacted information unless federal or state law authorizes or requires it (B)(1). response_type sets whole_denial (explain_denial, then possibly a complaint) or partial_denial (explain_partial_denial, then prepare_records releases the rest); an authorized redaction is not a denial and goes straight to prepare_records, which discloses it. The statute does not order the explanation and the release; the model explains first. Whether a redaction of information exempt under (A)(1) is itself 'authorized' by state law is left to the redaction_authorized_by_law input.

Costs: inspection carries no general fee, except that law enforcement agencies and prosecutors may charge the actual cost of preparing video records for inspection or copying, up to $75 per hour of video and $750 total, and victims who give the affidavit are exempt (B)(1), (B)(11). Copies are 'at cost' (B)(1), on paper, the medium the office keeps the record on, or another medium it can reasonably use, at the requester's choice (B)(6). The office may require advance payment of copy costs, postage, delivery and supplies (B)(6), (B)(7)(a). A policy may limit mailed or digital deliveries to ten per month unless the requester certifies a non-commercial purpose (B)(7)(c); 'commercial' is narrowly construed. For video records the estimate due within five business days is provide_video_cost_estimate; if its policy requires prepayment the duty to produce begins only on payment in full (pay_video_estimate); the caps, the 20% overage rule and the victim waiver are the video_fee table, which no task invokes. Missing the five-business-day estimate is treated as a division (B) failure that opens the complaint path; the statute states no other consequence. The video path is drawn before respond; the statute does not say whether the estimate precedes the response.

Requesters with special rules: incarcerated persons have no right to criminal investigation or prosecution records unless the sentencing judge finds the information necessary to support a justiciable claim (B)(8), modelled as the first response rule. Journalists may obtain certain information about designated public service workers by a signed written request stating the public interest (B)(9). Victims may obtain depictions of themselves (B)(10). The auditor of state may redirect requests for audit records to the original office (B)(1). Only (B)(8) is modelled.

Pre-suit complaint (C)(1): the aggrieved person must serve a complaint on the court of claims form under Civ. R. 4. The office then has three business days to cure, and the requester 'shall not file' within that period. cure carries an interrupting three-business-day timer whose expiry is the only way to file_suit, so a suit can never start inside the window; cure completing means the failure was resolved to the requester's satisfaction (failure_resolved). The office may 'cure or otherwise address the failure'; one that addresses it without satisfying the requester leaves cure open until the timer expires. (C)(2) restates the anchor: the complaint must have been transmitted 'at least three business days before the filing of the suit'. Consequence 'right-lapses' stands for the end of the office's pre-suit cure window, not a loss of the right to cure later.

One remedy, not both (C)(1): file_suit stands for either a complaint with the clerk of the court of claims or common pleas under § 2743.75, or a mandamus action in common pleas, the court of appeals, or the supreme court. Each must be filed with a written affirmation that the complaint was served, the failure is unresolved, and at least three business days passed (C)(2); without it the suit 'shall be dismissed'. The outcome gateway must be read in the order written: suit_dismissed (no_affirmation), then claims_complaint (chose_court_of_claims), then writ_denied, otherwise mandamus_judgment. Likewise the gateway after submit_request is read in order: request_ambiguous, law_enforcement_video_request, aggrieved, otherwise respond.

Mandamus remedies (C)(3)-(6) are tables that no task invokes, because the court is outside the agency process: statutory_damages; court_costs (mandatory to the relator on a compliance order or a (C)(4)(b)(iii) bad-faith finding, and the office may recover costs and expenses if a denied writ was frivolous, (C)(4)(a), (C)(6)); and attorney_fees (discretionary on a compliance order or a (C)(4)(b)(i)-(iii) ground, barred when both (C)(4)(c) well-informed-office conditions hold, office's fees if frivolous). The (C)(5) limits on fees (only fees incurred before release plus fees litigating the fees, reducible where an alternative means should have been pursued) are summarised, not modelled.

Office duties outside a single request: keep records organised and the retention schedule available (B)(2), adopt and post a public records policy (E)(2), and send elected officials to attorney-general training (E)(1). These are standing duties, not steps in the request.
